the notes." "I'd have spent them. What happened to him?" "He was tried again for breaking out
of prison and was made a prisoner for life." I would have jumped down from the coach
to be left in darkness on the highway except that I knew the convict had no clue
to my identity. I had grown up so much and was dressed so differently now; I no
longer resembled the boy in the pub. Still, the coincidence of our being on the same coach
was strange enough to fill me with dread. For this reason I resolved to get off the
coach as soon as we reached town. I threw my little suitcase off the coach, got down
after it, and was left at the first lamp on the first stones of the town pavement.
I walked to the Blue Boar Inn and ordered my dinner. When the waiter recognized me, he
asked if he should send for Mr. Pumblechook. "No, certainly not." The waiter seemed surprised and soon brought
an old newspaper and laid it in front of me. I picked it up and read a
paragraph that reminded me of what Joe had told me during his visit. It said that a
certain corn merchant in town (that would be Pumblechook) had been the earliest friend of a certain youth
(that would be me) and was now his benefactor. "Even if I traveled as far as the
North Pole," I thought, "someone would insist that Pumblechook was my oldest friend and the source of
my fortune." The next morning I was up and out early. It was too soon to go to
Miss Havisham's, so I wandered through the countryside on her side of town, which was not Joe's
side. I could go visit him tomorrow. As I walked, I thought of Estella. Miss Havisham had
adopted Estella; she'd more or less adopted me; and it must be her intention to bring us together.
She was leaving it to me to restore the desolate old house, let sunshine into the dark
rooms, set the clocks going, and tear down the cobwebs. In short, I would do all the
shining deeds of a romantic young knight and, of course, I would marry the princess. I knew Estella
was not perfect, but I loved her against all reason. I found her irresistible. I had planned
to arrive at Miss Havisham's at my usual time. After I had rung the bell, I turned
my back on the gate, trying to catch my breath and keep the beating of my heart quiet.
I heard the side door open and footsteps come across the courtyard, but I pretended not to
hear even when the gate swung open on its rusty hinges. Someone touched my shoulder, and I
turned. I was startled to find myself confronted with the last person I'd expected to see working as
a porter at Miss Havisham's. "Orlick!" I cried. "Have you left Joe's forge?" "Does this look like
a forge?" he retorted. We walked to the house. "There never used to be a porter here,"
I said as we stopped in his rooms near the door. "Word got out there were no men
here, and it came to be considered dangerous with convicts in the area. I was recommended as
a strong man who could protect the place." Over his fireplace I noticed a gun decorated with
brass. "That gun's loaded," said Orlick. I didn't want to have any more conversation with him. "Should I
go up to Miss Havisham?" "How should I know? My orders end here." I turned down the
long, dark passage and went upstairs to Miss Havisham's room. I knocked on the door. "That's Pip's
knock," I heard her say. "Come in, Pip." She was in her chair near the old dressing table.
Sitting near her was an elegant lady whom I had never seen. In her hand she was
holding one of Miss Havisham's wedding shoes. I kissed Miss Havisham's hand. "Well?" she said in a
grimly playful manner. I didn't know what she expected me to say. "I heard that you were so
kind as to wish to see me." "Well?" she said again. The other lady put down the
shoe and looked up at me. Estella! But she was so changed and much more beautiful. As
I looked at her, I felt I had slipped hopelessly back into being a coarse and common
boy. Estella gave me her hand. "Do you find her much changed?" Miss Havisham struck her walking stick
on a chair that stood between them. It was a sign that I should sit there. "When
I came in, I saw nothing of Estella in the face or figure, but—" "She was proud
and insulting," Miss Havisham interrupted, "and you wanted to get away from her. Don't you remember?" I said
that was long ago and I knew no better then. Estella smiled and said she had no
doubt that I was right about her being disagreeable. "Is he changed?" Miss Havisham asked her. "Very
much," said Estella. "Less coarse and common?" said Miss Havisham, playing with Estella's hair. Estella looked at me
and laughed. We sat in the strange, old room and I learned that she had just come
home from France and was going to London. It was settled that I would stay there all
day, return to the inn at night, and to London tomorrow. Miss Havisham urged us to go out
and walk in the neglected garden. So Estella and I went out. I was trembling inside and
worshiping the very hem of her dress. She was quite composed and most decidedly not worshiping the
hem of my garments. We drew near the place where I had fought Herbert. "I must have been
a strange little creature to hide and watch you fight that day," she said. "You rewarded me
afterward," I said. "Did I?" She'd obviously forgotten that she'd let me kiss her. "I remember I
was upset because your opponent had been brought here to pester me with his company." "He and I
are great friends now." "Since your change of fortune, you've changed your companions. What was fit company
for you then would be quite unfit company now," she said in a haughty voice. I don't
know if I had had any intentions left of visiting Joe, but after her remarks, I had none.
We strolled through the garden and around the brewery. I asked if she remembered how she had
brought me food and that she'd made me cry. "Did I? You must know that I have
no heart, and that may have something to do with my memory. I mean I have a physical
heart. But I have no softness there, no sympathy." She stood still and looked attentively at me.
What was I seeing in her looks and gestures? Something I'd seen in Miss Havisham? Or in
someone else? We walked back into the house and Estella went to dress for dinner, leaving me with
Miss Havisham. "Is Estella beautiful? Do you admire her?" "Everyone who sees her must admire her, Miss
Havisham." She put her arm around my neck and drew my head down close to her as
she sat in her chair. "Love her, love her, love her! If she is kind to you, love
her. If she wounds you, love her. If she tears your heart to pieces, love her!" I
could feel her thin arm tighten around my neck. "Hear me, Pip! I adopted her to be
loved. I made her into what she is to be loved. Love her!" She said the word "love."
But even if the word had been "hate," it could not have sounded more like a curse.
Mr. Jaggers came to Miss Havisham's to dine that night.
Miss Havisham did not join us, and Mr. Jaggers explained that she never let anyone see her eat or drink.
"She wanders during the night. That's when she gets something to eat."
Later we played cards with Estella and Miss Havisham, and it was agreed that I would meet Estella's coach when she came to London.
That night Mr. Jaggers and I stayed at the Blue Boar Inn.
I lay awake, thinking of Estella and wondering when she would begin to be interested in me.
The next morning at breakfast I resolved to tell Mr. Jaggers that I didn't think Orlick was the right sort of person to fill a position of trust at Miss Havisham's.
"Very good, Pip," said Mr. Jaggers when I had finished. "I'll go back today and pay him off."
I was alarmed that Mr. Jaggers was going to dismiss Orlick so quickly.
I even hinted that Orlick might be difficult to deal with.
"Oh no, he won't," said Mr. Jaggers. "I'd like to see him argue with me."
Later that day we traveled back to London together.
As soon as I arrived in the city, I sent a codfish and a barrel of oysters to Joe to apologize for not visiting him.
At Barnard's Inn I found Herbert having a cold supper.
He was delighted to welcome me back, and after eating we sat in front of the fire and talked.
"Herbert, I have something to tell you. I love—adore—Estella."
Instead of being surprised, Herbert said, "Of course I know that
." "How do you know that? I never told
you." "You didn't have to tell me. You've adored her ever since I've known
you. But now I must say something disagreeable to
you. Think of how she was brought up. Think of Miss Havisham. Think of how Estella is
herself. This may all lead to misery. Can't you forget
her?" "No! It's
impossible!" "You can't
try?"
"No!" An uncomfortable silence fell between us. Herbert got up and busied himself with tidying the room, putting chairs back where they belonged and straightening up
books. Finally he came back and sat down near the fire. "Now I must tell you something. I am engaged, but it's a
secret." "May I ask her
name?"
"Clara." "Does she live in
London?" "Yes, she lives with her father, an invalid. I've never seen him because he keeps to his room upstairs, but I've heard him constantly. He roars and he pounds on the floor with some frightful
instrument." "Don't you expect to see
him?" "Oh yes, I constantly expect to see him. I never hear him without expecting him to come tumbling through the ceiling." Herbert laughed at his
joke. He told me that the moment he made enough money, it was his intention to marry this young
lady. As we stared at the fire, I thought about how difficult it was to make enough
money. The days passed, and one day when I was busy with my studies, I received a note in the
mail. Although I had never seen the handwriting before, I knew it was from
Estella. She said that she would be arriving in London the day after tomorrow and asked me to meet her
coach! If there had been time, I probably would have ordered several suits of clothes for this
occasion. But since there wasn't time, I had to be content with what I
owned. My appetite vanished and I knew no peace until the day
arrived. In her traveling dress, Estella seemed more beautiful than ever.
Her manner was more charming toward me than ever before.
We stood near the inn while she pointed out her luggage to me.
When it was all collected, I remembered that I knew nothing of her destination.
"I'm traveling ten miles to Richmond," she said. "I am to have a carriage and you are to take me. This is my purse and you are to pay my expenses from it."
I hesitated to take her purse.
"Oh, you must take the purse!" she insisted. "We have no choice, you and I, but to obey our instructions. We are not free to follow our own minds."
As she looked at me, I hoped there was some hidden meaning in her words.
"A carriage will have to be sent for, Estella. Will you stay here a little?"
"Yes, I am to stay here, and I am to drink some tea, and you are to take care of me."
She put her arm through mine as if that were part of the instructions too, and we went into the inn for some tea.
"Where are you going in Richmond?" I asked when we were seated at a table.
"I'm going to live at great expense with a lady who has the power to take me around and introduce me to a lot of people. How do you enjoy living with Mr. Pocket?"
"I live quite pleasantly there, at least . . . ," I hesitated, ". . . at least as pleasantly as I could anywhere away from you."
"You silly boy," Estella said quite calmly. "How can you talk such nonsense?"
And then she went on talking about Matthew Pocket and his family.
Apparently there were others in the family who regularly gave Miss Havisham bad reports about me.
But Estella said I should not worry because nothing could make Miss Havisham dislike me.
Estella, in fact, was entertained by the efforts of these relatives to discredit me.
She playfully gave me her hand and I put it to my lips.
"You ridiculous boy," she said. "You should have asked before you touched my hand."
"May I kiss your cheek?"
"If you like."
I leaned down, and her calm face was like a statue's.
"Now," said Estella, gliding away the instant I kissed her cheek, "you are to take me to Richmond."
We got into a carriage and began our journey. When we passed through Hammersmith, I showed her where Mr. Matthew Pocket lived.
I said it wasn't far from Richmond and that I hoped I would see her sometimes.
"Oh yes, you are to come when you think it's proper. You have already been mentioned to the family."
"I'm surprised that Miss Havisham could part with you again so soon after your return from France."
"It's part of her plans for me, Pip," said Estella, sighing as if she were tired.
"I am to write to her constantly and see her regularly and report on how I'm doing."
That was the first time she'd ever called me by my name, and I treasured it.
We arrived at the house in Richmond all too soon. Two maids came fluttering out to receive Estella. The doorway soon absorbed her boxes.
She gave me her hand and a smile and was then absorbed into the house too.
After the door shut, I continued to stand there, looking at the house.
I thought about how happy I would be if I lived there with her.
Yet I knew I was never happy with her. I was always miserable.
I usually spent about half the week at Hammersmith studying with Matthew Pocket. And when I was there,
I also visited Richmond where Estella was staying. The rest of the week I was in London
with Herbert. Herbert and I spent as much money as we could and as a result we began
to run into debt. Sometimes I would say to him, "My dear Herbert, we are getting on badly.
Let us look into our financial affairs." We always felt great satisfaction from making an appointment for
this purpose. We ordered something special for dinner, and after dinner we took out a bundle of pens,
a large supply of ink, and plenty of paper. I would take a sheet and write at
the top, "Memorandum of Pip's debts," and Herbert would do the same. We then consulted our piles of
unpaid bills. When I had put all my debts on my list, I compared each with its bill
and checked it off. Then I folded up all my bills and tied them into a neat
bundle. After one of these sessions, we always felt that we'd put our affairs in order, even though
we hadn't paid a single bill. We shut our door on these occasions so that we wouldn't be
interrupted. One evening we heard a letter drop through the slot in the door. "It's for you,"
said Herbert, picking up the letter and looking at its heavy black seal and border. "I hope nothing
is the matter." But I opened the letter and found that my sister had died. Whatever my
fortunes might have been, I could not recall my sister with much tenderness. But I was seized with
a violent indignation against the assailant who caused her to suffer so much in recent years. With sufficient
proof I could have pursued Orlick or anyone else to the end of the world. I went
home for the funeral, and my sister was laid quietly in the churchyard close to the graves of
my father and mother. Afterward Biddy, Joe, and I had a cold dinner, but we dined in the
best parlor, not in the old kitchen. Joe was so careful about what he did with his
knife and fork and the salt that I felt a terrible restraint between us. But after dinner when
I went to the forge with him, we got along better. We sat down outside the forge. He
was very pleased when I asked if I could sleep in my own room. I was pleased
too, for I felt I'd done a great thing in making the request. When the evening shadows were
closing in, I took the opportunity of going into the garden with Biddy for a little talk.
"I suppose it will be difficult for you to remain here, Biddy?" "Oh, I can't do so, Mr.
Pip. It wouldn't be proper," said Biddy in a tone of regret mixed with quiet conviction. "How are
you going to live? If you want any money . . ." "How am I going to
live?" repeated Biddy. "I'm going to try to get the position of teacher in the new school." She
smiled. "You know, Mr. Pip, I learned a good deal from you after we were in school together,
and I've had time since then to improve." "I think you would always improve under any circumstances."
I walked a little farther, looking silently at her. "No one has told me the details of my
sister's death." "She had not spoken for a long time, but that evening she said, 'Joe.' She
made signs that she wanted him to sit close to her and wanted me to put her arms
around his neck. I did so and she laid her head on his shoulder. Soon she said 'Joe'
and once 'pardon' and once 'Pip.' And then she never lifted her head again." Biddy cried and
the darkening garden was blurred in my own sight too. "Nothing was ever discovered about the night she
was attacked?" "Nothing, Mr. Pip." "Do you know what has become of Orlick?" "I think from the color
of his clothes that he's working in the quarries." "So you've seen him then. Why are you
looking at that tree in the lane?" "I saw him there on the night she died, and I
have seen him there since we've been walking here." I started to run from the garden, but
Biddy laid a hand on my arm to stop me. "He was only there a minute and now
he's gone." It revived my anger to learn that Orlick was still pursuing Biddy. I told her that
I would spend any amount of money or do whatever was necessary to drive him away. By
degrees Biddy calmed me. She told me how Joe loved me and never complained about anything but always
did his duty with a strong hand and a gentle heart. She didn't say he never complained about
me, but I knew that’s what she meant. "We must speak of these things again," I said,
"for, of course, I shall be down here often. I'm not going to leave poor Joe alone." Biddy
said nothing. "Biddy, do you hear me?" "Yes, Mr. Pip." "Your constant calling me Mr. Pip is in
bad taste," I went on. "What do you mean?" "What do I mean?" asked Biddy timidly. "Now
don't echo me. You didn't used to echo. I made a remark about coming down here often to
see Joe, which you received with deliberate silence. Have the goodness to tell me why." "Are you
quite sure that you will come to see him often?" asked Biddy, stopping in the narrow garden path
and looking at me with clear and honest eyes. "Don't say any more, if you please, Biddy. It
shocks me that you would say such a thing." I kept Biddy at a distance and then
went up to my room. When I was restless in the night, which was every quarter hour, I
reflected on what an unkindness, what an injury, what an injustice Biddy had done to me. Early in
the morning I was to leave. I looked in one of the forge windows and saw Joe
at work. I went into the forge to talk to him. "Good-bye, dear Joe." I held out my
hand. "No, don't wipe off your hand. I shall be down soon and often." "Never too soon,
sir," said Joe, "and never too often, Pip." Biddy was waiting for me at the kitchen door with
a mug of milk and a crust of bread. I gave her my hand as I left. "Biddy,
I am not angry, but I am hurt." "No, don't be hurt," she pleaded. "Let me be
hurt if I have been ungenerous." Once more the mist was rising as I walked away from home.
Herbert and I continued to add to our debts. We looked forward to my twenty-first birthday because
we felt sure that my guardian, Mr. Jaggers, would reveal something about my fortune on that occasion. When
I arrived at his office that day, Mr. Jaggers was standing in front of the fire. We
shook hands and he told me to take a seat. He remained standing with his back to
the fire. "Now, my young friend," he said, "I am going to have a word or two with
you. How much do you think you spend per month?" "Per month, sir?" "Yes, per month." Despite
the fact that Herbert and I often reviewed our finances, I had to confess that I had
no idea how much I spent. "I thought so!" Mr. Jaggers blew his nose with an air
of satisfaction. "Now that I have asked you a question, do you have anything to ask me?" "Is
my benefactor to be made known to me today?" "No. Ask another." "Am I to learn that
information soon?" "Wait on that one and ask me another question." I looked around, but there seemed
no possible escape from the next question. "Do you have anything for me?" "I thought you'd ask that!"
Mr. Jaggers said triumphantly. He called for his clerk, Wemmick, who brought him a slip of paper.
Mr. Jaggers handed the paper to me. It was a banknote for five hundred pounds. "Now that's
a handsome sum of money," said Mr. Jaggers. "It's a birthday present, and you are to live on
that sum per year until your benefactor appears. Instead of coming here and asking me for money,
you will now be in charge of your affairs." I began to express my thanks to my
benefactor when he stopped me. "I am not paid to carry your words to anyone." After a
pause I returned to the question that he wouldn't answer earlier. "Is it likely that my benefactor will
soon come to London or ask me to appear somewhere else?" Mr. Jaggers stared at me. "We
must go back to the evening when we first met in your village. What did I tell
you then?" "You told me that it might be years before that person appeared." "That's right. And that
is my answer. When that person appears, you and that person will settle your affairs. My part
in this business will be over." We looked at each other until I looked away. "If that
is all you have to say, sir, then there is nothing left for me to say." I took
my leave of him and went into the outer office, where Wemmick was preparing to go home.
I wanted to ask his opinion because an idea had come into my head as soon as
I received the banknote. "Mr. Wemmick, I would like to help a friend." Wemmick shook his head as
if he were dead set against any weakness of this sort. "This friend," I continued, "is trying
to succeed in commercial life but has no money. I want to help him get started." "Mr.
Pip, I could name six bridges on the Thames River for you. Take a walk upon any
of them, pitch your money into the Thames, and that will be the end of it. Give money
to a friend and that will be the end of it too." "This is very discouraging," said
I. "It's meant to be. A man should never invest money in a friend." "And that is
your final opinion?" "That's my final opinion in this office." I sensed a loophole. "Would that be your
opinion at home?" "Home is one place, and this office is another. You are welcome to visit
my father and me at home." And so on Sunday I went to visit him. Wemmick's small
wooden house stood out from the others nearby. The top had been painted to look like the top
of a castle. A drawbridge, made from a wooden plank, spanned a ditch in front of the
house. It was one of the smallest and most unusual houses I'd ever seen. I knocked on
the front door, and Wemmick's father answered. Wemmick was out walking. I sat down but it was
difficult to have a conversation because Wemmick's father was hard of hearing. Suddenly I was startled by a
click in the wall near the chimney. A little wooden flap marked "John" tumbled open. "My son!"
the old man cried triumphantly. "It's our signal that he has arrived home." We went out to
the drawbridge to meet Wemmick, who was accompanied by a woman named Miss Skiffins. Her gown was a
little too orange and her gloves were a little too green, but she seemed to be a
regular visitor to the unusual little house and was very kind to Wemmick's father. I complimented Wemmick
on his ingenious device, the flap he used for announcing himself. He disappeared into another room, and presently
there was another click and a flap marked "Miss Skiffins" tumbled open. "Mr. Wemmick made them with
his own hands," Miss Skiffins confided to me. "The secret of the flaps is known only to
my father, Miss Skiffins, and me!" said Wemmick when he rejoined us. Wemmick then invited me to take
a walk with him around the property. He showed me his flagpole and a small cannon that
he fired every night at nine o'clock. He also pointed out his garden and his pig, chickens,
and rabbits. "So if the place were besieged, we could hold out for a long time," he
explained. I seized this opportunity to speak to him about Herbert. I told him how we had met,
how Herbert had helped me settle into London, and how we lived together beyond our means. I
wanted to help him with his income now and gradually buy him a small partnership, all without
his knowledge of course. I laid my hand upon Wemmick's shoulder. "There's no one else in the world
who can advise me." Wemmick considered what I had said. "Well, you know, Mr. Pip, I must
tell you something. This is awfully good of you. Miss Skiffins' brother is an accountant. I'll look
him up and go to work for you." I had several meetings with Wemmick after that. We found
a worthy, young shipping broker named Clarriker, who was looking for intelligent help and money now, and
who would eventually want a partner. Through Miss Skiffins' brother, I arranged to pay 250 pounds and
make other payments later to buy Herbert’s share of the partnership. The whole business was so cleverly
arranged that Herbert never suspected my involvement. I will never forget his face when he came home one
evening and told me that a shipping broker was interested in hiring him. I had the greatest
difficulty restraining my tears of triumph when I saw him so happy. When he finally went to
work for Clarriker, he spent the whole evening talking to me, excited about his success. That night when
I went to bed, I really did cry to think that my great expectations had benefited somebody.
Estella was living with a widow named Mrs. Brandley, who had been a friend of Miss
Havisham's before she shut herself away. In and out of Mrs. Brandley's house, I suffered
every kind of torture that Estella could cause me. She made use of me to tease
other admirers—and she had many admirers. I saw her often at Richmond, and I heard of
her often in town. There were picnics, plays, operas, concerts, parties—all sorts of pleasures through
which I pursued her, and they were all miseries to me. I never had one hour's
happiness with her, and yet I was always thinking of the happiness we would have
if we were married. If that house in Richmond is ever haunted, it will surely be
haunted by my ghost. Oh, the many, many days and nights that my spirit wandered through
that house, though my body was elsewhere. One day Estella announced that Miss Havisham wished
to see her and that I was to accompany her. Miss Havisham seemed even fonder of
Estella now than before. She clung to Estella's hand and hung on Estella's every word. She
asked for names and descriptions of the men whom Estella had attracted. I realized bitterly
that Estella was meant to wreak Miss Havisham's revenge on men, and that she would not
be given to me until this had been accomplished. Miss Havisham had sent Estella out to
attract and torment men, knowing that Estella was beyond the reach of all these admirers.
We were seated by the fire when Estella began to withdraw her hand from Miss Havisham's
clutches. "What!" said Miss Havisham, flashing her eyes at Estella. "Are you tired of me?"
"Only a little tired of myself," said Estella, moving away. "Speak the truth, you ingrate!" cried
Miss Havisham, striking her walking stick on the floor. Estella looked at her with perfect calmness
and then looked down at the fire. Her indifference to Miss Havisham seemed almost cruel.
"Oh, look at her!" cried Miss Havisham bitterly. "Look at her, so unfeeling and thankless and
proud. You stone! You cold, cold heart!" "You should know," said Estella. "I am what you
have made me. Who taught me to feel nothing? Who praised me when I learned
my lesson?" "But to be proud and unfeeling to me !" Miss Havisham shrieked. She stretched
out her arms and sank to the floor. From the moment they began to argue, I
had wanted to leave the room. I left them now and walked about the courtyard
and the ruined garden for an hour or more. When I felt I could brave the
room again, I ventured upstairs. I found Estella sitting near Miss Havisham, stitching one of
the ancient bridal garments that had fallen to pieces. Later Estella and I played cards, and
there were no further arguments between the two of them that evening, or on the four
subsequent days when I accompanied Estella to Miss Havisham's. It is impossible to discuss this
time in my life without mentioning Bentley Drummle, although I would be glad not to speak
of him. At our friend Startop's suggestion, Herbert and I had joined a club called the
Finches of the Grove. I never discovered the purpose of this club. I only knew
that its members dined out twice a month at an expensive hotel and then quarreled among
themselves as much as possible after dinner. Unfortunately Drummle was also a Finch. One evening it
was Drummle's turn to toast a lady. While the decanters were going around the table,
I thought I saw him look at me in a sly manner. But since there was
no love lost between us, that look could have meant anything. I was stunned when
he called upon us to drink a toast to "Estella." "Estella who?" I challenged him. "Never
you mind," he retorted. "Estella of where? You must say where she is from." And that
was true; that was a club rule. "Estella of Richmond, gentlemen. A beauty without equal."
"I know that lady," said Herbert from across the table. "And so do I," I added
with a scarlet face. " Do you?" said Drummle. Provoked, I immediately stood up and said
that was so typical of Drummle, coming into the club and proposing a toast to
a woman he didn't know. But, alas, it turned out that he did know her. The
next day Drummle appeared at the club with a polite little note from Estella, acknowledging
that she had had the honor of dancing with him several times. I soon found out
that he was pursuing her, and our paths crossed every day. Estella sometimes encouraged him, sometimes
discouraged him. She flattered him; she openly despised him. But the Spider, as Mr. Jaggers
had called him, was used to lying in wait and held on. He had confidence in
the attraction of his money and his family's good name. At a ball in Richmond, where
Estella outshone all the other beauties, he hung around her so much that I resolved
to speak to her about him. I waited until the end of the evening when she
was sitting by herself, ready for Mrs. Brandley to take her home. "Estella, look at that
fellow in the corner who is staring at us." I nodded toward Drummle. "Why should
I look at him?" Estella kept her eyes on me. "He has been hovering about you
all night." Estella glanced at Drummle. "Moths and all sorts of ugly creatures hover about
a lighted candle. Can the candle help it?" "No, but can't you help it?" "Well, perhaps!"
she said with a laugh. "Listen to me, Estella. It makes me miserable that you encourage
a man who is so generally despised as Drummle. You know everyone hates him." "Well?"
"You know he is a bad-tempered, stupid fellow." "Well?" "You know he has nothing to recommend
him but money and a long line of ancestors." "Well?" she said again. Each time she
said it, she opened her lovely eyes wider. "I cannot bear that people would say,
'She throws herself away on a mere boor, the lowest in the crowd,'" I went on.
"I can bear it." "Oh, don't be so proud and inflexible, Estella." "You call me proud
and inflexible in one breath," she replied, "and yet you also reproach me for stooping
to a boor." "Because you do! I have seen you give him looks and smiles tonight
that you never give to . . . me." Estella turned to me, suddenly looking
serious. "Do you want me then to deceive and entrap you?" "Do you deceive and entrap
him?" I asked. "Yes, and many others. All of them but you. But here is Mrs.
Brandley, and I will say no more." She stood up to go, and I knew
that my eyes were not the only ones that followed her as she left the ballroom.
I was now 23 years old and I had not heard another word on the subject of
my benefactor. Meanwhile Herbert and I had moved to a house down by the river. But
business had recently taken Herbert away to France, and I sadly missed his cheerful conversation. The weather
was miserable: stormy and wet with deep mud in all the streets. Day after day a heavy
rain poured over London. We lived on the top floor, and the wind rushing up the river
shook the house at night. Occasionally smoke came rolling down our chimney and into the room
as if it couldn't bear to go out in such terrible weather. One night I read until
eleven o'clock. As I listened to the church bells striking the hour, I heard footsteps on the
stairs. I took my lamp out onto the landing. "Is someone down there?" I called out.
"Yes," said a voice from the darkness below. "Who are you looking for?" "Mr. Pip." "That's my
name." I stood with the lamp held over the stair rail, and a man came slowly into
view. He looked to be about sixty, with long, iron-gray hair and a face that was
browned by the sun. As he reached my door, he looked pleased to see me and to
my amazement held out both his hands to me. "What do you want?" I asked. "If you'll
let me come in, I'll explain." We entered the room, and he looked about him with an
air of pleasure as he pulled off his rough outer coat and hat. I motioned him
to a chair before the fire. "There's no one here?" He looked over his shoulder. "Why do
you, a stranger coming into my rooms at this time of night, ask that question?" "You're a
smart one." He shook his head at me with affection. "I'm glad to see you've grown
up to be a smart one." And suddenly I knew him! It was as if the wind
and rain had driven away the intervening years and once more I was in the churchyard with
my convict. He stood up and held out both hands again. I reluctantly gave him my
hands and he raised them to his lips. "You acted nobly, my boy, and I never forgot
it." Afraid that he was going to embrace me, I laid a hand upon his chest to
stop him. "Keep away. If you're grateful for what I did as a child, I hope you've
shown your gratitude by mending your way of life. It wasn't necessary to come here to
thank me. Surely you must understand . . ." "Understand what?" "That I do not wish to
renew our acquaintance. But you are wet and you look weary. Would you drink something before you
go?" He nodded and I poured him a drink. When I gave him the glass, I
noticed his eyes were full of tears and my attitude toward him softened. I quickly poured myself
a drink and sat down. "How are you making a living?" I asked him. "I've been a
sheep farmer and a stock breeder in Australia. I'm famous for how well I've done." "Have
you ever seen the messenger you sent to me bearing two one-pound notes?" "Never saw him again."
"They were a small fortune to a poor boy. But like you I've done well since then,
and you must let me pay them back. You can give them to another poor boy." He
watched me as I took out two notes and handed them to him. Still watching me,
he folded them together lengthwise and burned them over the lamp. "May I be so bold as
to ask how you have done so well, Pip?" He stood up and went over to the
fireplace. "I was chosen to receive some money from a benefactor." "Might I ask who this
benefactor is?" I faltered. "I don't know." "Could I guess what your income has been since you
turned 21? Is the first figure a 5?" With my heart beating like a hammer, I stood
up and looked wildly at him. "You must have had a guardian before you were 21.
Probably a lawyer. Would the first letter of his name be J ?" The truth of my
situation came flashing in on me, and I had to struggle to breathe. "You're probably wondering how
I discovered where you live. When I arrived in England, I wrote to someone for your address.
That person's name? Wemmick." I could not have spoken one word even if my life depended
on it. I stood with a hand on a chair and a hand on my chest when
the room began to spin, and I thought I would faint. He caught me and led me
over to the sofa. "Yes, dear Pip, I've made a gentleman of you! I've worked hard
so you would never have to work. I'm your second father!" In his triumph he did not
notice my reaction. "Look here!" He took my watch out of my pocket. "This is a gentleman's
watch. Look at your clothes and all your books!" He kissed my hands again while my
blood ran cold. "Didn't you ever think it might be me?" "Oh, no, no, never." "No one
was involved except myself and Mr. Jaggers. How good-looking you've become! Is there a bright-eyed lady somewhere
that you love to think about?" "Oh, Estella! Estella!" I thought. "If there is such a lady,
then you shall have her, dear boy. Not that a gentleman like yourself can't win her
on your own, but you shall have the money to back you." Desperately I wished that he
had left me at the forge! "Where will you put me to sleep tonight?" he asked, looking
around. "My friend is away. You must have his room." I rose from the sofa. "He
won't come back tomorrow, will he? Caution is necessary." "Caution?" "I was sent to serve a life
sentence in Australia. I would certainly be hanged if captured." This miserable man had risked his life
to come to me, and now I was responsible for him! I quickly locked the door
and closed the window shutters so no light could be seen from outside. Then I showed him
to Herbert's room, where he took me by both hands to say goodnight. I got away from
him and sat down in front of the fire. Miss Havisham's plans for me were all a
dream. Estella was never meant for me. But worst of all, it was for this convict—guilty
of some unspoken crimes—that I had deserted Joe. In every surge of wind and rain, I heard
pursuers. Twice I thought someone knocked at the door. I remembered what a violent man he had
seemed to me as a child, and a terrifying thought began to form: it was not
safe to be alone with him. I crept softly to Herbert's room and locked my convict inside.
I resolved to tell people that the convict was my uncle who had arrived unexpectedly from
the country. I fell asleep in my chair by the fire, and when I awoke, the
church bells were striking five. The fire and candles had gone out, and the wind and
rain intensified the thick, black darkness. I reached around but could not find a way of getting
a light, so I decided to go to the watchman's room and ask him to come
with his lantern. I stumbled down the dark staircase and fell over something. A man! Startled,
I asked, "What are you doing here?" There was no response as the man moved silently
away from me. I ran to the watchman's room and urged him to come quickly. It
troubled me that someone had been lurking on the stairs on this night of all nights.
I asked the watchman if he had let anyone in. "The night being so bad, sir,
few people have come through my gate. I don't recall another person since about eleven o'clock
when a stranger asked for you." "My uncle," I muttered. "And the person with him." "Person with
him?" "When your uncle stopped at the gate, a man stopped and followed him this way."
The watchman hadn't noticed what sort of person this man was except that he was wearing
dust-colored clothes under a dark coat. When I returned to my rooms, my mind was very
troubled by the man on the stairs. I lighted my fire and fell into a troubled
doze. At breakfast the next morning, I thought my convict looked even worse by daylight. "I
don't even know what name to call you," I said as he took his seat at
the table. "I've said that you're my uncle." "That's it, dear boy! Call me uncle." "I
suppose you’ve assumed some name?" "Yes, I’ve taken the name of Provis." "What's your real name?" "Abel
Magwitch." "When you asked the watchman the way here, was anyone with you?" "I think there
was a person who came in with me." I worried that he was being followed. "Are
you known in London?" "I hope not! I was mostly in the provinces." "Were you on
trial in London?" He nodded. "The last time. Mr. Jaggers was my lawyer. That's how I
met him." It was on my lips to ask what crime he'd been tried for, but
he said, "And I've paid for what I've done." Then he started in on his breakfast.
If I'd had any appetite, he took it away. I sat and watched him eat. Afterward
he filled his pipe and lit it from the fire. He turned around and held out his
hands to me. "And this is the gentleman I've made. It does me good to look
at you, Pip." He laid a great pocketbook bursting with notes on the table. "There's more
money where that came from. I've returned to see my gentleman spend his money like a
gentleman." "Stop!" I cried in a frenzy of fear and dislike. "I want to know how
you're to be kept out of danger. How long are you going to stay?" "How long?"
He took his pipe from his mouth and his jaw dropped. "I'm not going back. I've
come for good." Once more he took me by both hands and surveyed me with an
air of proud ownership. It seemed that the best thing I could do was to secure him
some quiet lodging nearby. He would then have a safe place to go when Herbert returned
in a few days. I discussed with him what clothing he should wear. We agreed that
he would dress like a prosperous farmer and that he would cut his hair short. It
should have been a simple matter to act on these precautions. But in my distracted state,
I didn't get out to act on them until mid-afternoon. He was to remain in my
rooms while I was gone and not open the door to anyone. I knew of a
respectable lodging house on Essex Street, so I went there and secured the second floor for
him. I then went from shop to shop, making purchases that were necessary for the change in
his appearance. That being accomplished, I did another errand on my own behalf. Mr. Jaggers was
at his desk, but when I entered the room, he immediately got up and stood in
front of his fire. "Now, Pip, be careful. Don't tell me anything. I don't want to
know anything." "Mr. Jaggers, I merely want to assure myself that what I have been told
is true. I've been informed that a man named Abel Magwitch is my benefactor. Is he
my only benefactor?" "The only one." "I am not unreasonable, sir, so I do not think
you are responsible for my mistakes and wrong conclusions. But I always thought my benefactor was
Miss Havisham." Mr. Jaggers coolly turned his eyes toward me. "As you say, I am not at
all responsible for that. When I communicated with Magwitch in Australia, he hinted in his letter
at seeing you here in England. I cautioned him that I must hear no more of
that. He was not at all likely to obtain a pardon. He was sent away for
life and returning to this country would render him liable to the extreme penalty of the
law. No doubt he took my advice." "No doubt." "I have been informed by Wemmick that
he received a letter from someone named Provis asking for your address on behalf of Magwitch.
Wemmick sent him the information. It is through Provis that you received the information about Magwitch?"
"It came through Provis," I replied. "Good day, Pip. Glad to have seen you." Mr. Jaggers offered
me his hand. "When you write to Magwitch in Australia—or communicate with him through Provis—tell him
that the remainder of your account will be sent to you." The next day the clothes
I had ordered arrived and Provis put them on. The better I dressed him, the more
he looked like the fugitive on the marshes. Perhaps this was because his old face and
manner were growing familiar to me. But I also believed that he dragged one leg as
if there were still an iron on it. From head to foot, there would always be
something of the convict about him. At the same time, he was a dreadful mystery to
me. When he fell asleep in a chair, I studied him, wondering what he had done. I
loaded him up with all possible crimes until I had a powerful impulse to flee. I
doubt if a ghost could have seemed more terrible. But a ghost could not be arrested
and hanged because of me. The dread that Provis would be discovered added to my horrors.
One evening after dinner, I heard footsteps on the stairs. Provis heard them too, and in an instant
I saw a jackknife shining in his hand. "It's Herbert!" I said as my friend came bursting into
the room. "How are you, Pip! I feel like I've been gone for a year. You look quite
thin and pale! Pip, my dear fellow . . ." The sight of Provis stopped him. Provis
was slowly raising the jackknife and groping in another pocket for something else. "Herbert, my dear friend." I
shut the door while Herbert stood wondering what was going on. "Something very strange has happened. This is
. . . a visitor of mine." Provis pulled a small black book out of his pocket and
made Herbert swear on it that he would not reveal anything he heard. I can't begin to describe
Herbert's astonishment when he and I and Provis sat down near the fire and I began to recount
the whole secret. I saw my own feelings reflected in his face. Although I was anxious to talk
to Herbert alone, Provis seemed to want to stay with us. It was after midnight when I finally
walked Provis back to his own door. Never quite free from my uneasiness about the man on
the stairs, I always looked around when I took my "uncle" home. When I returned home, Herbert received
me with open arms. Never before had I felt so blessed to have a friend. We sat back
down in front of the fire. "What can I do?" I asked. Herbert held his head. "I am
too stunned to think." "So was I when Provis first arrived. He is intent upon various new expenses
for me—horses, carriages. He must be stopped somehow." "You mean you can't accept any more money?" "How can
I? Think of him." We both shuddered. "And think of what I owe him already!" I continued. "I
am heavily in debt and have no expectations. I'm fit for nothing except, perhaps, to be a
soldier." Here I broke down and Herbert seized my hand. "Don't say you're fit for nothing," said Herbert.
"I suppose you could renounce his patronage and become a soldier with some hope of repaying him. But
that's a very faint hope indeed. Besides, it's absurd for you to become a soldier. You would be
infinitely better with me at Clarriker's, small as it is. I'm working up toward a partnership, you know."
Poor fellow! He did not suspect that this had happened with my money. "But there's another issue," said
Herbert. "He's a determined man who has long had one fixed idea. More than that, he seems to
be a fierce and desperate character." "I know he is." And I told Herbert the story of Provis
fighting with the other convict on the marshes years ago. We agreed that if I cut Provis
out of my life, he might be so disappointed that he would let himself be captured. In a
way this would make me his murderer. I was so struck by the horror of this idea that
I couldn't sit still and began pacing. "The first thing you must do," said Herbert, "is get him
out of England. You will have to go with him in order to persuade him to go." "But
what is to prevent him from coming back?" "I don't know. Get him out of England and then
we'll figure out how to get you away from him." We shook hands on that. "He is so
bound up with my fortunes and misfortunes, and yet I know nothing of him," I said. "Except
as the miserable wretch who terrified me for two days in my childhood." "Then you must ask him
at breakfast," said Herbert. And with that plan, we went to bed. The next morning Provis came for
breakfast, and when we had finished eating, I said, "Last night I told Herbert about the struggle you
were engaged in when the soldiers found you on the marshes. Can you tell us something about that
other convict?" Provis lit his pipe and began his story. More than twenty years ago he'd met a
man named Compeyson at the races. "That's the man you saw me fighting with on the marshes." Compeyson
was a handsome smooth-talker who'd been raised as a gentleman. Provis became his business partner. "And what
was Compeyson's business?" said Provis. "Swindling, forging signatures, passing stolen bank notes, and things like that." There was
another man named Arthur who had also worked with Compeyson, but he was sick and dying. "He and
Compeyson had been in a bad situation with a rich lady years before, and they'd made a pot
of money from it. But Compeyson had gambled it all away." Compeyson was letting Arthur live with him,
but he was also keeping a careful account of the dying man's room and board, in case Arthur
ever got well enough to pay him back. Compeyson left it to his wife to take care of
Arthur. According to Provis Arthur raced into Compeyson's parlor one night. "She's upstairs with me and I can't
get rid of her," said Arthur. "She's all in white with white flowers in her hair and
she's awfully mad." "You fool," said Compeyson. "How could she be up there? We would have seen her
come through the door!" "I don't know," said Arthur. "But she's standing at the foot of my bed,
awfully mad. And where her heart's broken— you broke it!—there are drops of blood." Compeyson was always a
coward, so he told Provis to help his wife put Arthur back to bed. Still screaming about the
woman in white, Arthur died the next morning. "Now as to what Compeyson did after that," said Provis,
"I'll simply say that I was always in debt to him, always under his thumb, always working, always
getting into danger." Eventually the two of them were caught. Compeyson immediately asked that they be tried
separately. "I was so poor, I had to sell all my clothes to hire a lawyer," said Provis.
But Compeyson appeared in court dressed as a gentleman. He gave as much evidence as he could against
Provis. The judge felt Compeyson was a good person who'd fallen in with bad company, so Compeyson got
seven years in prison and Provis got fourteen years. "I threatened him," said Provis. "We were sent to
the same prison ship and we both escaped one night. When the soldiers captured us, he claimed he
fled because I was trying to kill him. Once more his punishment was light. But I was put
on trial again and sentenced for life." "Is Compeyson dead now?" I asked after Provis finished his story.
"I never heard of him again." Provis stood up and took a drag on his pipe. While
Provis talked, Herbert had been writing in the cover of a book. He softly pushed the book over
to me as Provis stood smoking and looking at the fire. I opened the book and read Herbert's
note: Miss Havisham's half brother was named Arthur. Compeyson is the man who was to marry Miss Havisham.
Provis' story caused a new fear to grow in my mind: If Compeyson were still alive,
he might discover that Provis had returned to England. I knew that I must take Provis abroad
as soon as possible because Compeyson would waste no time turning him over to the police.
I told Herbert that I must see both Estella and Miss Havisham before I left England. But
when I went to Richmond, I found that Estella was away visiting Miss Havisham. So the
next day, I set off for home by the early morning coach. When I arrived at the
Blue Boar Inn, the first person I saw was Bentley Drummle! We pretended not to see
each other. It was a very lame pretense because we both went into the coffee room, where
he had just finished his breakfast and where I ordered mine. It pained me to see
him in town for I knew why he was there. I pretended to read an old
newspaper at my table while he stood in front of the fire. But after a while, I
got up, determined to have my share of the warmth. In order to stir the fire,
I had to reach behind him for the poker. "Are you acting like you don't know me?"
said Drummle. "Oh, it's you. I was wondering who was blocking the fire." With that, I
gave the fire a tremendous poke and planted myself by his side, my shoulders squared and my
back to the fire. "You've just arrived?" Drummle edged me a little away with his shoulder.
"Yes." I edged him a little away with my shoulder. "This is a beastly place," he
said. "Your part of the country, I think?" "Yes, I'm told it's very much like Shropshire, where
you grew up." "Not at all. There are large tracts of marshes near here, I believe?"
"Yes, what of it?" "I'm going out for a ride to explore those marshes. Remote villages there,
they tell me. Curious little pubs and blacksmiths. Waiter! Is that horse of mine ready?" "Yes,
sir," said the waiter, hurrying over to us. "He's being brought around to the door." "The lady
won't ride today because the weather's bad," said Drummle. "And I won't dine here tonight because
I'm going to dine at the lady's." "Very good, sir." Drummle glanced at me with an insolent
triumph. I knew we couldn't go on much longer without mentioning Estella by name. And choked
and boiling as I was, I couldn't bear to hear him say her name. "Mr. Drummle,
I did not seek this conversation, and I don't think it's an agreeable one. I suggest that
we have no further communication in the future." "I quite agree. But don't lose your temper.
Haven't you lost enough without that?" Before I could respond, he went out and mounted his horse.
He called for a light for his cigar. A man in dust-colored clothes appeared, and as
Drummle leaned down from the saddle and lit his cigar, something about the man reminded me of
Orlick. I washed my face and hands and then went out to the old house that
I wished I'd never seen. I found Miss Havisham seated by the fire in her gloomy
room. Estella was knitting as she sat by Miss Havisham's feet. "Miss Havisham," I began, "I'm as
unhappy as you could ever have meant me to be." Miss Havisham looked steadily at me;
Estella did not raise her eyes from her knitting. "I have found out who my patron is.
It's not a discovery that is likely to enrich me in any way. However, I must
say no more of that because it's another person's secret. Why did you let me believe you
were my patron, Miss Havisham? Was that kind?" Miss Havisham struck her walking stick on the
floor and said angrily, "Who am I to be kind? What else do you have to say?"
"I started to help my friend Herbert Pocket two years ago without his knowledge. Why I
cannot continue is part of someone else's secret. But if you could spare the money to
help him, I would tell you how to do something useful and good." Miss Havisham stared into
the fire for a long time. Then she said, as if there had been no pause
in our conversation, "What else?" I turned to Estella and tried to control my trembling voice. "You
know that I have always loved you." Estella raised her eyes to me but showed no
emotion. "I thought Miss Havisham meant us for one another," I went on. Estella shook her head.
"I know I have no hope of ever calling you mine. I don't yet know how
poor I am or where I'm going. But I still love you." "When you say you
love me, you touch nothing in my heart. I've tried to warn you of this, have I
not?" "Yes," I said miserably. "Is it true that Bentley Drummle is pursuing you? That you
encourage him and ride out with him and that he will dine with you today?" She seemed
surprised that I knew all this but said, "All quite true." "You cannot love him. You
would never marry him, would you, Estella?" She looked toward Miss Havisham and then studied her knitting
for a moment. "Why not tell you the truth? I'm going to be married to him."
I dropped my face into my hands, but I was able to control myself better than I
expected, considering the agony her words caused me. When I raised my face, there was a
ghastly look upon Miss Havisham's face. "Dearest Estella, do not let Miss Havisham lead you into
this fatal step. Refuse me forever, but bestow yourself on some worthier person than Drummle. Miss Havisham
gives you to him as a great injury to the many far better men who admire
you." Estella responded in a gentle voice. "The preparations for my marriage have begun, and I shall
be married soon. Do not blame Miss Havisham. It is my own decision." "Your own decision
to fling yourself away on such a mean and stupid brute? Even if I remained in England,
how could I see you as Drummle's wife?" "Nonsense. You will get me out of your
thoughts in a week." "Out of my thoughts! You are part of my existence, part of
my self." She offered me her hand and my bitter tears fell upon it. I held her
hand to my lips. "God bless you, Estella. God forgive you!" And so I left her.
I remembered later that Estella looked at me with wonder while Miss Havisham—her hand covering her heart—gave
me a horrible stare of pity and remorse. So much was done and gone; outside, the
light of the day seemed much dimmer now. I decided to walk back to London because I
wanted to tire myself out. It was past midnight when I crossed London Bridge. As I
passed through the gate to our lodgings, the porter handed me a note. On the outside was
written, Please read this here. I opened it and read in Wemmick's writing: Don't go home.
As soon as I read the warning from Wemmick, I took a carriage to Covent Garden, where
I was able to get a room for the night. I got into bed and lay there, weary
and miserable, unable to sleep. What had happened? When would I be able to go home? Was
Provis safe? These questions occupied my mind so busily that there was no room in it for
anything else. Even when I thought of Estella and how we had parted that day forever, I couldn't
forget Wemmick's warning: Don't go home. I had left instructions that I should be awakened at seven
o'clock. It was obvious that I must see Wemmick and that I must see him at his
house. The night had been so miserable, I was relieved to get out of the room. By eight
o'clock I was crossing the drawbridge at Wemmick's fortress. "Hello, Mr. Pip!" said Wemmick, who was in
the middle of making breakfast for his father and himself. "So did you go home then?" "Yes,
but I received your note and didn't go inside." "Would you mind cooking this sausage for my father?"
He handed me the sausage and I held it over the fire. "Yesterday morning at Newgate Prison,"
said Wemmick, "I accidentally heard that somebody—we won't name this person—had caused quite a stir by leaving
Australia and never being heard from again." I was so nervous that I accidentally lighted the sausage like
a torch and had to blow it out. "I also heard that you had been watched at
home and might be watched again." "By whom?" I asked. "I can't go into that," said Wemmick
quickly. "It might clash with my official responsibilities." He took the sausage from me and brought it to
his father along with some bread and tea. I realized that he couldn't tell me some things
out of loyalty to Mr. Jaggers. When he returned, I told him that I was determined to
ask him some questions, but whether he answered them or not was up to him. He nodded. "You
have heard of a man of bad character whose name is Compeyson?" Wemmick nodded. "Is he living?"
Wemmick nodded again. "Is he in London?" Wemmick gave me one more nod. "Now question time is
over. Let me tell you what I did. When I couldn't find you yesterday, I went to Clarriker's
to find Mr. Herbert. I told him that if he was aware of somebody being around your
rooms or in the immediate neighborhood, he should get that somebody away while you were out of
town." By "somebody" I understood him to mean Provis. "At first Mr. Herbert did not know what to
do because I said there is no safer place to hide than a large city." Then Herbert
had told Wemmick that he was courting a young lady who lived with her bedridden father in
a house farther down the river. The house was kept by a widow named Mrs. Whimple who had
a furnished upper floor for rent. "I thought it would be a good idea to move somebody
to this house," said Wemmick. "First of all, it's away from your usual spots. Secondly, Herbert will
be able to bring you news of somebody without having to go there. Thirdly, if you should eventually
want to slip somebody aboard a foreign ship, there he is—ready." Having finished his breakfast, Wemmick looked
at his watch and began to get his coat on. "And now, Mr. Pip, I have probably done
all I can do. Here is the address. It's the house with the bow window." He handed
me a slip of paper. "There can be no harm in going there tonight to visit somebody.
If you have nothing more to do, I advise you to stay here until dark." And so I
spent the day dozing in front of the fire with Wemmick's ancient father. At eight o'clock I
went out in search of the house at Mill Pond Bank. "All is well," said Herbert, when
I was inside the house. "My dear girl is with her father. When she comes downstairs, I'll introduce
you. That's her father." I had become aware of an alarming growling overhead. "He's a sad, old
rascal. To have Provis for a lodger is a blessing for Mrs. Whimple because most people wouldn't
stand that noise." While we were talking, a very pretty girl of twenty or so came downstairs, and
Herbert introduced her as Clara Barley. She was a most charming girl, and I was looking at
her with admiration when suddenly the growling upstairs swelled into a roar. "Papa wants me, darling," Clara
said as she ran away. Herbert and I went upstairs and found Provis comfortably settled in his rooms
at the top of the house, from where he had a good view of the river. I
had decided to say nothing about Compeyson for fear that Provis might rush out to track him
down. When I had explained everything that Wemmick had told me, I asked Provis whether he relied on
Wemmick's judgment and sources of information. "Yes, dear boy," he said seriously. He seemed to have mellowed
in his new home. "When the time comes, I will go abroad with you," I said. "Or
follow shortly afterward, if Wemmick thinks that might be safer." "Pip, we are both good watermen," interjected Herbert.
"When the right time comes, we could take him down the river ourselves. We would not have
to hire a boat or any boatmen. It might be a good thing if you started to
keep a boat and got in the habit of rowing up and down the river. If you fall
into this habit, then no one will notice you." I liked this scheme, and Provis was elated.
We agreed that whenever he saw us on the river, he would pull down his window blind
as a signal that all was well. Once everything was arranged, I rose to go, remarking to Herbert
that we should not be seen going home together. "I don't like to leave you here," I
said to Provis, "though you are certainly safer here than near me. Good-bye!" "Dear boy." He clasped
my hands. "I don't like to say good-bye. Say good night!" "Good night! Herbert will go regularly between
us, and when the time comes, you may be certain I'll be ready." Everything was quiet when
I arrived home. Herbert came home half an hour later and looked out the window. There was
no one on the pavement. The next day I got a boat and began to go out on
the river, sometimes with Herbert, sometimes by myself. I was often out in cold, rain, and sleet,
but nobody took much notice of me after a while. I frequently saw the window blind rolling
down as I passed Mill Pond Bank. Herbert was at the house three times a week and never
brought me any alarming news. Still, I could not get rid of the sense of being watched.
A few weeks passed without bringing any change. We waited for a sign from Wemmick, but there was
nothing. My financial affairs began to wear a gloomy appearance, and I was pressed for money by
more than one creditor. I began to feel a lack of money and relieved it by converting some
jewelry into cash. But I had determined it would be wrong to take more money from Provis, so
I gave Herbert the unopened pocketbook to return to him. As time wore on, an impression settled
heavily upon me that Estella was married. Fearful of having this confirmed, I avoided the newspapers and begged
Herbert never to speak of her to me. It was an unhappy life I was living, dominated
by my anxiety that Provis would be discovered and captured. Condemned to inaction and a state of constant
restlessness and suspense, I rowed about in my boat and waited, waited, waited as best I could. One
afternoon late in February, I came ashore at dusk. Both going down the river and returning, I
had seen Provis' signal at the window. All was well. As it was a chilly evening and I
was cold, I comforted myself with dinner. And as I had hours of dejection and solitude before me
if I went home, I decided to see Mr. Wopsle, my old friend from the country, perform
at the theater. The evening's performance consisted of two plays. The second one was a grand comic piece
in which Mr. Wopsle played the part of an enchanter. He had a good deal of time
on his hands since the enchanter's role seemed primarily to be talked at, sung at, danced at, and
flashed at with fires of various colors. I observed that he devoted his time to staring in my
direction as if he were lost in amazement. There was something so remarkable in Mr. Wopsle's stare
that I was still thinking about it after the performance. When I came out of the theater, he
was waiting for me. "I noticed that you saw me in the audience," I said as we walked
down the street together. "Of course I saw you, and I saw him too." "Him?" Wopsle's mysterious
words gave me a chill, and I looked around to make sure no one was following us. "Oh,
he's not in sight," said Mr. Wopsle. "He went out of the theater before I left the
stage. I had a ridiculous idea that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw that
you were quite unconscious of him sitting behind you like a ghost." I was so distrustful in those
days that I even suspected this poor actor was trying to get me to betray Provis. Therefore
I glanced at him as we walked along but said nothing. "Mr. Pip, remember a certain Christmas Day
when you were a child, and I dined at Joe Gargery's house with you, and some soldiers came
to the door to get a pair of handcuffs mended?" "I remember it very well." "And you
remember that there was a chase after two convicts, and that we joined in? And do you remember
we came upon the two convicts fighting on the marshes?" "Yes." "Well, Mr. Pip, one of those
two convicts sat behind you tonight." My heart began to pound. "Which one do you think you saw?"
"The younger one," said Mr. Wopsle. "The one who cried out that the other was trying to murder
him." "This is very strange," I said, trying to appear as if it meant nothing to me.
But I cannot exaggerate the terror I felt at knowing that Compeyson had sat behind me like a
ghost. Ironically, the only time he had not been in my thoughts since hiding Provis was in those
very moments when he was closest to me. I asked Mr. Wopsle many questions, and after he
had answered them and I had treated him to some refreshments, we parted. When I reached home, I
looked around, but no one was on the street. Herbert and I had a very serious talk
by the fire. We agreed that I must write to Wemmick of the evening's events and remind him
that we were waiting for him to take action. About a week later, Mr. Jaggers invited Wemmick and
me to dine at his house. "Wemmick, did you send that note of Miss Havisham's to Mr.
Pip?" Mr. Jaggers asked soon after we sat down at the table. "Here it is," said Wemmick, handing
the note to Mr. Jaggers. "I did not send it once I knew we would be dining together
tonight." Mr. Jaggers passed the note on to me. "Miss Havisham says she wants to see you
on a little matter of business you mentioned to her. You'll go soon?" "I have another engagement," I
said, glancing at Wemmick, "that makes me uncertain of my schedule. But I'll try to go at
once." Mr. Jaggers' housekeeper brought a dish to the table. "How slow you are today, Molly," he said.
As Molly withdrew her hands from the dish, she fell back a step or two, nervously muttering some
excuse. And a certain motion of her fingers as she spoke drew my attention. The motion was
like the act of knitting. She stood looking at her master, not understanding whether she was free to
go or whether he had more to say to her. Her look was very intent. I looked at
those hands; I looked at those eyes; I looked at that flowing hair. I compared them to
other hands, other eyes, other hair that I had seen recently. And I felt absolutely certain that this
woman was Estella's mother. After dinner Wemmick and I left together. "Wemmick," I said as we walked
along. "Do you remember telling me the first time I went to Mr. Jaggers' house to notice his
housekeeper? You called her a wild beast tamed. How did Mr. Jaggers tame her?" "That's his secret. She
has been with him many years." "I wish you would tell me her story." "I don't know
all of her story, but I'll tell you what I know. Twenty years or so ago, that woman
was on trial for the murder of another woman and was acquitted. Molly was a handsome young woman,
and she had been married very young. She was accused of killing the other woman out of
jealousy, and Mr. Jaggers was her lawyer. It was also said that she had destroyed her three-year-old child
as revenge against her husband. But she was never put on trial for that." "And has she
been in Mr. Jaggers' service ever since?" "Yes," said Wemmick. "Do you remember the sex of the child?"
"It was said to have been a girl." "You have nothing more to say to me tonight?" "Nothing
more than I got your letter and destroyed it." We exchanged a cordial good night, and I
went home. I had many new things to think about, but still no relief from my old thoughts.
When I went to visit Miss Havisham, she was not in her room but in the larger
room across the passage. I found her sitting by the hearth in a ragged chair, lost in
contemplation of the fire. There was an air of utter loneliness about her. And I thought
how over time, I too had become a part of the wrecked fortunes of this house. As
I sat down in another of the ragged chairs, I noticed a new expression on her face;
it was as if she were afraid of me. "I want to pursue that subject you mentioned
to me when you were last here," she said, "and to show you that I am
not all stone. But perhaps you can never believe that there is anything human in my heart."
I said some reassuring words and she continued. "You said that you could tell me how to
do something useful and good for your friend." I began explaining to her the history of Herbert's
partnership at Clarriker's. But she seemed lost in thought, so I stopped speaking. "Do you break off
because you hate me too much to speak to me?" Once again she looked as if
she were afraid of me. "No, I stopped because I thought you were not following what I
said." I went on to tell her how I had hoped to complete the transaction with my
own money. This was no longer possible, but I could not tell her any more without revealing
the secrets of another person. She nodded. "And how much money is needed to complete the
purchase of the partnership?" "Nine hundred pounds." It sounded like such a large sum. "If I give
you the money for this purpose, will you keep the secret of my patronage as you have
kept your own?" "Quite faithfully." "And your mind will be more at rest?" "Much more at rest."
"Are you very unhappy now?" She asked this question without looking at me, but in an
unusual tone of sympathy. I could not reply for a moment because my voice failed me. "I
am far from happy, Miss Havisham, but I have other causes of discontent than the one you
know of. They are the secrets I have mentioned." "Can I only serve you, Pip, by serving
your friend? Is there nothing I can do for you?" "Nothing, but I thank you for asking."
With that, she wrote a letter to Mr. Jaggers, directing him to pay me the money.
She read me what she had written and then handed me the letter. "My name is on
the first page. If you can ever write under my name, 'I forgive her,' please do it."
"Oh, Miss Havisham, I can do it now!" To my amazement—I may even say to my terror—she
dropped on her knees at my feet with her folded hands raised to me. I entreated
her to rise, but she only pressed my hand and began to cry. I had never seen
her shed a tear before. "Oh! What have I done!" she cried despairingly. "If you mean what
have you done to injure me, let me say, very little. I would have loved Estella under
any circumstance. Is she married?" "Yes. She is in Paris now. I didn't know what I had
done until you spoke to her during your last visit, and I saw in you a
reflection of what I had once felt. What have I done! What have I done!" "Miss Havisham,"
I said when her cry had died away. "You may dismiss me from your conscience. But Estella
is a different case, and if you can ever undo any scrap of what you have done
to her, you should." "Yes, I know. But, Pip, my dear!" There was real compassion in
her new affection for me. "You must believe this: when she first came to me, I meant
to save her from misery like my own. At first I meant no more." "Well, I should
hope so." "But as she grew and became very beautiful, I stole her heart away and put
ice in its place. If you knew my story, you would have some compassion for me." "I
believe that I do know your story, and I hope I understand it and its influences.
Because of what has passed between us, may I ask you a question about Estella? Not as
she is, but as she was when she first came here?" Miss Havisham nodded. "Go on." "Whose
child was Estella?" "I don't know." "Mr. Jaggers brought her here or sent her here?" "He brought
her here, and I called her Estella. I had been shut up in these rooms a
long time when I told Mr. Jaggers that I wanted a little girl to raise and love
and save from my fate. He told me that he would look about for an orphan child."
"Might I ask her age at that time?" "Two or three. She knows nothing except that she
was an orphan and I adopted her." I was now convinced that Mr. Jaggers' housekeeper, Molly, was
Estella's mother. What more could I achieve by prolonging this conversation? I had succeeded in securing
Herbert's partnership, and Miss Havisham had told me all she knew of Estella. Twilight was closing in
when I went down into the courtyard. I made my way to the ruined garden. I went
by the corner where Herbert and I had fought; I went by the paths where Estella and
I had walked. It was all so cold, so lonely, so dreary. I went back to
say good-bye to Miss Havisham, who was now sitting in the ragged chair close to the fire.
In the moment when I was about to leave, a great flaming light sprang up. She ran
at me, shrieking, with a wall of fire blazing all around her. I tried to smother the
flames from her dress with my coat. I dragged the cloth from the table for the
same purpose and with it dragged down the heap of rottenness in the middle. For a moment
we were on the ground, struggling like desperate enemies. She shrieked wildly and tried to free herself
as I held her down until the servants came running. When the doctor arrived, I was astonished
to see that both my hands were burned. I had felt nothing. Miss Havisham was seriously injured
and she was laid upon the table. There was a time that evening when she spoke
calmly of what had happened. But toward midnight her thoughts began to wander and she said repeatedly,
"What have I done?" And then, "When she first came, I meant to save her from misery
like mine." And then, "Take the pencil and write under my name, 'I forgive her!'" As I
could do no more there, and I had a more pressing reason for being at home,
I decided to leave by the early coach. At six in the morning, I leaned over Miss
Havisham and kissed her. "Take the pencil," she said, "and write under my name, 'I forgive her.'"
Both my hands and my left arm had been badly burned in the fire at Miss Havisham's.
Since my arm was in a sling, I could only wear my coat like a cloak,
loose over my shoulders. Herbert devoted the day to caring for me. He was the kindest of
nurses, taking off my bandages at regular intervals, steeping them in a cool liquid, and patiently putting
them on again. Neither of us spoke about how I could not row the boat now,
but we both were thinking of it. We agreed—without saying anything—to make my recovery a matter of
hours instead of weeks. My first question for Herbert, of course, was whether all was well
with Provis. He replied in the affirmative, and we did not return to the subject until later
in the evening. "I sat with Provis last night for two good hours," said Herbert. "Where was
Clara?" "Tending to her father all evening. I doubt that he will live much longer." "And
then you will be married?" "Yes. Lay your arm upon the back of the sofa, and I'll
take your bandage off. Provis was very talkative and told me more about his life," said Herbert.
"Tell me every word!" Herbert removed the bandage. "It seems he was married to a young
woman who was jealous and revengeful." "How revengeful?" "She was put on trial for murdering another woman.
Mr. Jaggers defended her and that is how Provis first heard of him." "Was she found guilty?"
"No, she was acquitted," said Herbert. "She and Provis had a little child of whom Provis
was exceedingly fond. On the night of the murder, she swore to Provis that she would destroy
the child and he would never see the child again. Then she vanished." By this point Herbert
had my arm bandaged again and back in the sling. And I had more questions for
him. "Did she keep her oath?" I wanted to know. "That remains the darkest part of Provis'
life. She did." "That is, he says she did." "Well, yes, my dear boy," said Herbert.
"I have no other source of information. She had shared four or five years of the miserable
life that he described to us. He felt pity for her, and fearing that he would have
to testify about this destroyed child, he hid during the murder trial. Even though he grieved
for his child, he didn't want his wife to be sentenced to death. And so there was
only some vague talk about a man named Abel Magwitch being the cause of the jealousy that
had led to murder." "But what happened after his wife was found not guilty?" "After the
acquittal she disappeared, and thus Provis lost the child and the child's mother. That evil genius, Compeyson,
knowing that Provis had remained hidden during the trial, used that information to work him harder. It
became clear to me that this was the main reason that Provis hated Compeyson." "Herbert, I
need to know if Provis told you when this all happened." "He said it took place about
twenty years ago. And he said that when he met you in the churchyard, you reminded
him of the little girl he so tragically lost." After a short silence, I asked Herbert to
feel my forehead. "You do not think that I have a fever or that my head is
muddled by last night's accident?" "No, my dear boy," said Herbert. "You are rather excited but
you are quite yourself." "I know I am quite myself. And the man we have been hiding
down the river is Estella's father." Herbert was as astounded as I was at this revelation, but
he reacted more calmly than I did. I was seized with a frantic need to settle
the matter immediately. I could scarcely be restrained from going out to Mr. Jaggers' house that night
to find out the truth. But Herbert said if I did so, I would probably be completely
useless at the time when Provis needed me to row the boat. That thought alone reined
in my impatience. I agreed to stay at home that evening and rest my injured hands and
arm. Early the next morning, I went to Mr. Jaggers' office and found him going over
the accounts with Wemmick. I had sent him a brief description of the fire as soon as
I arrived in town. But now I went into more detail. When I had finished my story
and answered his questions, I produced Miss Havisham's note authorizing me to receive nine hundred pounds
for Herbert. "Did you ask Miss Havisham to do anything for you ?" said Mr. Jaggers. "No,
but I asked her some questions about her daughter. I believe I know more about her daughter
than Miss Havisham does." I paused. "I know who Estella's mother is." Mr. Jaggers looked at
me inquiringly. "Estella's mother?" "Yes, I've seen her within the past few days, and you've seen her
even more recently." "Really?" Mr. Jaggers continued to look at me coolly, but I thought I detected
a slight uneasiness in his manner. "Perhaps I know more of Estella's history than even you
do," I said. "I know her father too. He is the man named Provis from Australia." Even
Mr. Jaggers looked startled when I said those words. I dared not look at Wemmick to see
his reaction for fear that Mr. Jaggers would realize we communicated outside this office. "On what
