evidence does Mr. Provis make this claim?" asked Mr. Jaggers. "He doesn't make this claim because he
has no knowledge that his daughter is alive." Then I told Mr. Jaggers all I knew
and how I knew it. His only response was to turn to Wemmick and ask, "What account
were we at when Mr. Pip came in?" But I would not be put off like that.
I appealed to him to tell me the truth. "I am admitting nothing," said Mr. Jaggers.
"Do you understand that?" "I do." "Now, Pip, imagine that a woman, under such circumstances as you
have described, concealed her child and had to communicate that fact to her legal adviser as part
of her defense. Imagine that at the same time, an eccentric, rich lady had asked him
to find a child for her to adopt." "I follow you, sir." "Imagine that this legal adviser
lived in an atmosphere of evil where all the children he saw ended up being neglected, whipped,
imprisoned, and sometimes even hanged. What if there was one pretty little child who could be
saved from that life?" I nodded. "I understand." "Imagine the mother and father, unknown to one another,
were now living near each other. Imagine the child was now grown up and married for
money. Imagine that this secret was still a secret. For whose sake would you reveal it? The
father's? The mother's? The daughter's? It would hardly serve the daughter to learn about her parents and
drag her back to disgrace after an escape of twenty years." I did not have any
answers for his questions. "Now, Wemmick," said Mr. Jaggers, "where were we when Mr. Pip came in?"
With the check for nine hundred pounds in my pocket, I went to see Miss Skiffins' brother, who had arranged for Herbert's position at Clarriker's.
He brought Clarriker to me, and I had the great satisfaction of completing the arrangements for Herbert's partnership.
This was the only good thing I had done since I learned of my great expectations.
Clarriker informed me that his shipping business was steadily improving, and with the money from me, he would now be able to establish a small branch office in Egypt.
Herbert, in his new capacity as partner, would go out and take charge of it.
I felt as if my last anchor were loosening and I would soon be driven by the winds and the waves.
But I had some consolation knowing that Herbert would soon come home and tell me this news himself, little suspecting that I had been involved in it.
It was now March. My left arm was taking so long to heal that I was still unable to get a coat on. My right hand was tolerably restored.
One Monday morning, while Herbert and I were at breakfast, I received a note from Wemmick: Burn this as soon as you read it. On Wednesday you might do something if you feel able to try it.
Herbert and I considered what to do because my injury was now a real issue.
"I've thought it over," said Herbert. "Instead of taking a waterman to help us row, we should take Startop. He was my father's student and he likes us."
"But how much would you tell him about what we're doing?"
"Very little. He doesn't need to know until Wednesday morning that there's an urgent reason for getting Provis away. Where will you go with Provis?"
It seemed to me that the place didn't matter as long as Provis was out of England. Any foreign steamer that would take us would do.
Because foreign steamers left London at high tide, our plan was to get down the river earlier in the day and lie waiting in some quiet spot.
But we needed to know when a steamer would pass by.
After breakfast we went out to pursue our investigations and found that a steamer bound for Hamburg, Germany, would likely suit our purposes.
We also noted what other foreign steamers would leave London on the same tide.
I then went to secure passports while Herbert went to see Startop.
When we met again at one o'clock, I had the passports and Herbert had found Startop, who was willing to help us.
Herbert was going to Mill Pond Bank that evening to prepare Provis to meet us on Wednesday.
We would not communicate with Provis again until we took him on board my small boat.
When I went home, I found a letter, which had been delivered by hand:

If you are not afraid, come to the marshes tonight or tomorrow night at nine. Come to the little house by the kiln if you want information regarding your uncle Provis. Tell no one. You must come alone. Bring this letter with you.
I didn't know what to do. The worst was that I had to decide quickly or I would miss the afternoon coach, which would take me down in time for tonight.
Finally I decided to go because of the reference to Provis.
I left Herbert a note, saying that I had gone to visit Miss Havisham to see how she was faring, and then I hurried off for the coach.
It was dark before I arrived.
Avoiding the Blue Boar, where I might be recognized by someone, I went to another inn.
While my dinner was being prepared, I stopped briefly at Miss Havisham's and found that she was still very ill, though somewhat better.
Back at the inn, I was not able to cut my dinner because of my injured arm, so the landlord did it for me.
Not recognizing me, he entertained me with my own story—the popular local version that Pumblechook was my benefactor.
"Does this young man ever come back?" I asked about myself.
"Yes, but he never visits Pumblechook, the man who made him."
"And does Pumblechook complain about that?"
"Oh yes," said the landlord. "All the time."
I thought of long-suffering Joe and sweet-tempered Biddy, the ones who had the real right to complain about me.
I had never felt so remorseful about my thanklessness to Joe as that night when I heard about the brazen impostor Pumblechook.
After dinner I put on my coat and looked for the letter, but could not find it.
I had the uneasy feeling that I must have dropped it in the coach.
It was a dark night, though the full moon rose as I went out upon the desolate marshes.
I walked for another half hour before I approached the kiln and the little house.
I saw a light in the house and went in. There was a candle on the table but no one was there.
I stood just within the door, looking out into the night. Suddenly the candle went out and a rope was thrown over me from behind.
"Now I've got you!" said a voice.
"Who are you?" I cried, struggling as the man tied me up. "Help! Help!"
He struck a light and I was surprised to see Orlick.
"Do you recognize this?" Orlick picked up a gun decorated with brass that I had seen before at Miss Havisham's.
"You cost me that job. And you came between me and a young woman I liked."
Oh, Biddy! "What are you going to do to me?" I asked him.
"I'm going to kill you!" He leaned forward, staring at me. "You've been in my way ever since you were a child. And I'll tell you something else.
It was me who struck down your sister and left her for dead. But that's your fault.
You were always favored while I was bullied and beaten. You did that, and now you're going to pay for it."
I thought of crying out again, but I knew no one could hear me. My arms burned from the rope tied tightly around them.
"And I'll tell you one more thing," said Orlick. "It was me you tripped over that night on your stairs.
I've had a mind to kill you since you were down here for your sister's funeral.
I've followed you everywhere and when I looked for you, I found your uncle Provis!"
He held the candle close to my face and I turned away.
"I know his name is Abel Magwitch." He grinned malevolently. "Beware Compeyson. Beware the gallows."
He picked up a heavy hammer and I shouted out with all my might.
I struggled and suddenly I heard voices and saw men attacking Orlick.
He got free of them, leaped over the table, and flew out into the night. And then all went black and I knew no more.
When I regained consciousness, I found myself lying on the floor with my head on someone's knees.
I looked up and the face of the person supporting me came into view. "Herbert!" I cried. "And
Startop too!" "Stay quiet," said Herbert. "Don't be too eager to get up." I begged him to
tell me what had happened. Herbert said that he and Startop had returned to our rooms, where
they found the letter I had dropped. Worried for my safety, they took the next mail coach. "But
we couldn't find you in town," said Herbert. From the letter they knew I was headed for
the little house on the marshes. They found someone to guide them to the house, where they
came upon Orlick as he was about to attack me. When I told Herbert how Orlick had threatened
to kill me, he immediately wanted to get a warrant for Orlick's arrest. But I worried that
this would keep us in town, which might endanger Provis. So we went back to London that
night and I spent most of Tuesday asleep. Wednesday was one of those March days when the sun
shines hot and the wind blows cold. We had our pea coats with us, and I took
a bag with a few of my worldly possessions. As I stopped at the door and looked
back, I wondered when I would next see those rooms, or if I would ever see them again.
We went down to the river and got into my boat. My role was to steer while
Herbert and Startop rowed. My heart began to beat faster as we approached Mill Pond Bank. "Is
Provis there?" asked Herbert. "Not yet," I said. "Oh, wait. There he is." Herbert and Startop rowed toward
the stairs that led to the water. We touched the stairs lightly for a moment, and then
Provis was on board and we were off again. He had a seaman's cloak with him and
a black canvas bag, and he looked as much like a river pilot as I could wish. "Dear
boy!" Provis put his arm on my shoulder as he took his seat. "Faithful boy, well done.
Thank you!" We worked our way out into the river again, avoiding the bobbing buoys. Provis was
the least anxious of us, perhaps because of the miserable life he'd led. When danger came upon him,
he would confront it. Until then he didn't worry while I looked warily about for any sign
that we were arousing suspicion. With Provis securely wrapped in his cloak, we rowed all afternoon and
when darkness began to fall, we decided to pull up at the first lonely tavern we found. At
this dismal hour, we were all possessed by the idea that we were being followed. "What was
that noise?" one of us would whisper. "Is that a boat over there?" Afterward we'd fall silent
and I'd sit thinking what a lot of noise our oars made. At last we spied a light.
Stepping ashore I found the light to be in the window of a pub. It was a
dirty enough place but it would serve us for the night. After everyone had come ashore and
we had eaten dinner, we sat by the fire. The owner asked if we had passed a four-oared
galley with two passengers. We had not, but the galley had stopped at the pub, and the
owner had seen it going up and down the river all afternoon. I wondered why this galley
was hovering about in such an unusual way. We went to bed, but I slept poorly. On Thursday
afternoon, at the time we expected the Hamburg steamer, we rowed out into the middle of the
river. Half an hour later, we spied the smoke of a steamer with a second steamer right
behind it. They were coming at full speed, so Provis and I got our two bags ready and
said good-bye to Herbert and Startop. Neither Herbert's eyes nor mine were dry. Suddenly I saw a
four-oared galley shoot out from under a riverbank and row straight for us. The galley pulled closer
to us. One of the passengers was wrapped in a cloak much as Provis was. The other held
the rudder lines to steer the boat. No one said anything. After a few minutes, Startop could
make out which steamer was first. "Hamburg," he whispered. The steamer was nearing us very quickly, and
I felt as if its shadow were upon us. Suddenly the galley's rudder man shouted to us. "You
have a runaway prisoner there! The person in the cloak is Abel Magwitch, otherwise known as Provis.
I arrest him and call upon him to surrender!" Before we knew what was happening, the galley
had run into us and the passengers were holding onto our boat. There was great confusion aboard the
steamer, which was still bearing down on us. I heard the order given to stop the steamer.
I saw the galley's rudder man lay his hand on Magwitch. At that same moment, I saw
Magwitch lean across his captor and pull the cloak from the other passenger. Compeyson! And still at that
same moment, I saw Compeyson's face contort with terror, heard a loud splash, and felt the boat
sink from under me. It was only for an instant that I struggled underwater. Then I was
pulled on board the galley with Herbert and Startop, but our boat was gone and so were the
two convicts. The first steamer drifted away from us and the second passed us by. We all
looked at the water and presently a dark object was seen upon it: Magwitch swimming toward us.
He was taken on board and instantly handcuffed at the wrists and ankles. We rowed back to shore
and the pub that we had so recently left. Magwitch had received a very severe injury to
the chest and a deep cut on the head. I sat with him to comfort him. Magwitch
told me in a low voice that he and Compeyson had fallen overboard locked in each other's arms.
"We struggled fiercely, my boy, but I managed to swim away." We remained at the pub until
the tide turned, and then Magwitch was carried down to the galley. Herbert and Startop were scheduled
to return to London by land. When I took my place by Magwitch's side, I felt that this
was where I belonged as long as he lived. My horror of him had melted away and
I only saw a man who had behaved faithfully and generously to me over the years. I
only saw in him a much better man than I had been to Joe. I told him how
distressed I was that he had risked coming home for my sake. "Dear boy. You can be
a gentleman without me. It's best that you act as if you don't know me. I only
ask that you sit where I can see you at my trial." "I'll never leave your side," I
promised, holding his hand. "I will be as true to you as you have been to me."
I could not doubt that there were still people living who could identify Magwitch. I could not hope
that he would be treated leniently. I could foresee, however, that once he was convicted, the government of
England would take everything he owned. But there was no need to tell him that the money he
hoped to give me was gone forever. It would have crushed him to know that. Magwitch was taken
to court the next day to await the arrival of an old officer from the prison ship who
could identify him. Upon returning to London, I immediately went to see Mr. Jaggers with the idea of
hiring him to defend Magwitch. But Mr. Jaggers said there would be no way to defend Magwitch once
he was identified. The officer arrived three days later and identified Magwitch. His trial was scheduled for a
month later. It was at this dark time in my life that Herbert returned home one evening in
low spirits. "I fear I will soon have to leave you," he said. I was less surprised by
this news than he would ever know. "Clarriker's will lose a fine opportunity if I delay going to
Cairo," he said. "But I must ask you a question: have you thought about your future?" "I've been
afraid to think about it." "In this branch office, we must have a clerk . . . a
clerk who would one day become a partner just as I have done. Clara and I have talked
about this, and she begs me to say you must live with us in Egypt once we are
married. Will you consider it?" I thanked him. "Do you think, Herbert, that you could leave the question
unanswered for a while without doing any harm to your business?" "For a while!" cried Herbert. He seemed
delighted that I was even considering the question. "Six months, a year!" "Not so long as that," I
reassured him. "Two or three months at most." We shook hands on this agreement, and Herbert now had
the courage to tell me that he must leave at the end of the week. And so on
Saturday, I took my leave of Herbert, who was full of bright hope but sad and sorry to
go without me. Magwitch had broken two ribs, which had damaged his lungs, so he breathed with great
pain and difficulty. As a result he spoke very softly and he spoke very little. Being far too
ill to remain in the common prison, he was moved to the infirmary. This gave me opportunities to
be with him that otherwise I would not have had. I sometimes derived an impression from his manner
or a whispered word that he might have been a better man under better circumstances. When his trial
began, no one objected to my getting close to Magwitch and holding the hand that he stretched out
to me. The trial was very short. Some good things about him were said. He had taken up
industrious habits and had prospered lawfully and reputably in Australia. But nothing could change the fact that he
had returned to England. He was found guilty and sentenced to death. I began that night to write
petitions to men in authority who might be merciful toward him. I set forth my knowledge of him
and told how he had come back for my sake. For several days and nights after he was
sentenced, I was totally absorbed in these appeals and hardly slept. After I had sent them in, I
roamed the streets at night, wandering past the offices and houses of the men to whom I was
appealing. I earnestly hoped that Magwitch might die before his death sentence was carried out. My daily visits
to his bedside were shortened now and he was more strictly watched. Every day he seemed to grow
weaker. After about ten days, I saw a greater change in him than I had yet seen. His
face was turned toward the door, and his eyes lighted up when I entered. "Dear boy," he said
as I sat down by his bed. "I thought you were late but I knew you couldn't be.
You always wait at the gate, don't you?" "Yes, so I don't lose a moment of visiting time."
"Thank you, dear boy. God bless you! You've never deserted me." I pressed his hand in silence because
I could not forget that I had once meant to desert him. "And what's best of all is
you've been more comfortable alongside me since I was under a dark cloud than when the sun shone."
He lay on his back breathing with great difficulty. "Are you in much pain today?" I asked. "I
don't complain, dear boy." He had spoken his last words. He smiled and I understood that he wished
to lift my hand and lay it on his chest. I laid it there and he smiled again
and put both his hands upon it. "Dear Magwitch, I must tell you now at last. You understand
what I say?" There was a gentle pressure on my hand. "You had a child once whom you
loved and lost." There was a stronger pressure on my hand. "She lived and found powerful friends. She
is living now. She is a lady and very beautiful and I love her!" With a last, faint
effort that required my assistance, he raised my hand to his lips. Then he gently let it sink
onto his chest again, and he was gone. For a few days, I lay on the sofa or
on the floor—anywhere that I happened to sink down—with a heavy head and aching limbs. I had no
purpose and no power. I had scarcely any money and should have been alarmed by the state of
my affairs. But I knew nothing beyond the fact that I was falling very ill. Visions of boats
in a courtyard and Miss Havisham in a furnace came over me. I heard voices talking, laughing, and
groaning, and did not know if they were my own. At last I saw two men looking at
me. "I don't know you. What do you want?" I was startled that they were standing over me.
"Well, sir," said one of them, bending down and touching me on the shoulder. "You're under arrest for
debt." "How much?" I said weakly. "One hundred and twenty-three pounds owed to the jeweler. You'd better come
with us." I made some attempt to get up and dress myself. When I next noticed the men,
they were standing farther away but still looking at me. I just lay there. "I would come with
you if I could, but if you take me from here, I will probably die." Perhaps they replied.
I don't know what they said or did except they left me alone. That I had a fever
and often lost my reason cannot be denied. Someone took care of me. I did not know who
until one day I opened my eyes and saw Joe sitting on the window seat, smoking his pipe.
I'd fallen ill in April. Now, Joe informed me, it was the last day of May. When word
of my illness had reached Joe, Biddy had urged him to go to me at once. "What
about Miss Havisham?" I asked. "Is she dead?" "She is, and most of her property now belongs to
Estella," Joe said. He also told me that Orlick had been arrested for robbing Pumblechook's house. Joe stayed
on, and I grew stronger every day. Eventually I could walk by myself, and I began to
think of what I'd do next. As the days passed, I resolved to tell Joe about my change
in circumstances. But when I awoke one morning, I found a letter on the table. Not wishing to
intrude, I have departed because you are well again, dear Pip, and will do better without me.
–Joe P.S. Ever the best of friends. Enclosed was a receipt for my debt. Until that moment I'd
supposed that my creditor was waiting until I recovered to collect the money. But Joe had paid
it for me. I knew that I must follow him at once to thank him, and for another
reason: I'd decided to ask Biddy to marry me. I would leave it up to her whether I
would work at the forge with Joe or in Cairo with Herbert. So in a few days
I traveled to the countryside. I stayed overnight at the Blue Boar Inn, and while my breakfast was
being prepared, I strolled over to Miss Havisham's house. A sign on the gate announced an auction of
the household possessions and furniture. The house itself was to be knocked down and sold for building
materials. I felt like a stranger who didn’t belong there. After breakfast I set out for the forge.
The countryside seemed more beautiful and peaceful than ever before. As I walked along, I envisioned the pleasant
life that I could lead here with Biddy. When I reached the forge, I was puzzled to
find it closed. But the house was not deserted and the best parlor seemed to be in use
because there were white curtains fluttering in the windows. Suddenly Biddy and Joe were standing before me, arm
in arm. In a moment Biddy was in my embrace and we were both weeping with joy.
"Dear Biddy, how fine you look! And you too, Joe." I looked from one to the other and
then Biddy cried in a burst of happiness, "We were married today!" They took me into the kitchen
and I laid my head on the old table. Biddy held one of my hands to her
lips and Joe's hands were on my shoulders. "He wasn't strong enough to be surprised, my dear," Joe
said. They were both delighted that I had come to make their day complete! Thank goodness I'd
never told Joe my own plans for Biddy. I raised my head. "Dear Biddy, you have the best
husband in the world. And dear Joe, you have the best wife and she will make you as
happy as you deserve. I give you both my humble thanks for all you've done for me.
I'm leaving within the hour for I'm soon going to Cairo. I'll never rest until I've repaid you
the money that kept me from prison." Then I begged them to forgive me for having treated them
so miserably over the years. Joe wiped his eyes on his sleeve. "Dear Pip. God knows I
forgive you, if I even have anything to forgive." "And so do I," said Biddy. I went up

Within a month I was a clerk at Clarriker's in Egypt. Three months later Clara's father died,
and Herbert went home to marry her. Many years passed before I became a partner. When Herbert and
Clara returned to Cairo, I lived happily with them. I paid my debts and was in constant correspondence
with Biddy and Joe. It wasn't until I became a partner that Clarriker revealed to Herbert that
I'd provided the money for his partnership. Herbert was moved and amazed, but our friendship did not suffer.
Eleven years had passed since I last saw Biddy and Joe. One December evening I quietly opened the
kitchen door. I could see Joe smoking his pipe by the fire, and sitting in the corner
on my own stool, a boy who could have been me. There were cries of surprise when I
entered, and after I'd settled near the fire, Joe said, "We named him Pip after you. We
hoped he might grow up to be a bit like you." The next day I took young Pip
for a walk and found him to be a delight. Afterward I talked to Biddy as their other
child, a little girl, lay sleeping on her lap. "Biddy, you must give Pip to me sometime
or at least lend him to me." "No, no," she said gently. "You must marry." "That's what Herbert
and Clara say, but I don't think I will." Biddy looked down at her sleeping child. "Tell me
as an old friend. Have you quite forgotten Estella?" "I never forget anything of importance in my
life, but that poor dream has disappeared." Nevertheless I knew that I intended to visit the site of
Miss Havisham's house that evening for Estella's sake. I'd heard about her leading a most unhappy life and
being cruelly abused by her husband. And I'd heard of his dying in a riding accident. But
this had happened two years ago. For all I knew, she was married again. I walked out to
Miss Havisham's before dark. There was no house now, nothing but the wall of the garden. As I
stepped closer, I saw a woman walking on the garden path. "Estella!" "Pip! I'm so greatly changed.
I'm surprised you recognize me." We sat down on a nearby bench. "Do you often come here?" I
asked. "No. I'd intended to come back but never have. Poor old place." Tears filled her eyes. "The
grounds belong to me. It's the only possession I haven't relinquished. And you, do you still live
abroad?" "I do, and I work pretty hard for a sufficient living." "I've often thought of you." "Have
you?" "Yes. But I did not think that in leaving this place, I would leave you too.
I'm glad to do so." I looked at her in surprise. "You're glad to part again, Estella? To
me, the memory of our last parting is so painful." "But you said then, 'God bless you. God
forgive you.' Surely you can say that to me again now," Estella said earnestly. "Suffering has taught
me to understand what you felt. I've been bent and broken into a better shape. Please tell me
we're friends." "We are friends," I said as we rose from the bench. "And we'll continue to be
friends when we part." But as I took her hand in mine, and we walked out of
that ruined place, the evening mists rising around us, I saw no sign of another parting from her.
